# Overall Summary of Postsecondary Pathway Analysis This analysis examined what predicts postsecondary attendance and graduation for all 47,189 individuals in the dataset, and then what predicts credential level, institution type, and graduation location among the 24,998 who did complete a postsecondary credential. Together these outcomes map the full postsecondary sorting process for Southwest Minnesota high school graduates. ## **Who Goes to College and Who Completes** The data paint a clear and consistent portrait of who does and does not pursue and complete postsecondary education in Southwest Minnesota. Postsecondary attendance and graduation are strongly predicted by the same cluster of individual characteristics, and the gaps between groups are large. Students who are most likely to attend and complete postsecondary education are those who took the ACT (67.3% completion rate vs 26.6% for non-ACT takers), participated in PSEO (76.3% vs 36.5%), took AP exams (79.4% vs 48.6%), and scored higher on MCA Reading and Math. These students are also more likely to be female, non-special education, and not economically disadvantaged. In short, students who are academically prepared and college-oriented in high school are dramatically more likely to complete a postsecondary credential. Students who are least likely to attend and complete are those who did not take the ACT (53.6% did not attend at all), are identified as special education (59.6% did not attend, and of those who did attend only 21.7% graduated), are economically disadvantaged (42.4% did not attend, and only 34.6% of those who did attend graduated), are English learners (57.0% did not attend), or come from non-English speaking homes (48.5% did not attend). American Indian and Hispanic students also show notably lower attendance and graduation rates than their White, Asian/PI, and Black peers. Males are less likely than females to attend and complete at every stage. A critically important finding is that for most disadvantaged groups, the primary barrier is access rather than completion. Across special education status, economic status, English learner status, and non-English home language, the rate of attending but not completing postsecondary is nearly identical between disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged groups. What differs dramatically is whether students attempt postsecondary at all. This suggests that interventions focused on encouraging postsecondary attendance among disadvantaged groups may have greater impact than interventions focused on improving completion rates. CTE engagement shows a consistent and modest inverse relationship with postsecondary attendance and graduation. CTE Concentrators or Completors show lower postsecondary graduation rates (50.6%) than CTE Participants (55.2%) or No CTE students (56.4%), and take significantly more CTE courses than those who go on to graduate. This is not evidence of a negative outcome — it reflects the sorting of CTE-engaged students into direct workforce entry rather than postsecondary pathways, consistent with the regional workforce retention findings throughout this analysis. Geographic and local labor market variables show virtually no association with who attends or completes postsecondary education. Whether a student comes from EDR 6E, 6W, or 8, or from an entirely rural, town/rural mix, or urban/town/ rural mix community, has negligible bearing on their postsecondary pathway. Individual-level characteristics overwhelmingly determine who goes to college and who completes, not where in Southwest Minnesota they grew up. Local unemployment rates show a small association consistent with the opportunity cost hypothesis — students from lower unemployment areas are slightly more likely to enter the workforce directly — but the effect is negligible in practical terms. ## **Where College Completers Go and What They Earn** Among the 24,998 individuals who did complete a postsecondary credential, a second and equally clear sorting process determines what kind of credential they earn, what type of institution they graduate from, and where that institution is located. The portrait of a bachelor degree or higher completer at a 4-year institution outside the Southwest Minnesota region is quite specific: they took the ACT (ACT takers show a 67.6% bachelor degree or higher rate vs 21.0% for non-ACT takers among completers), participated in PSEO (71.4% vs 40.4%), took AP exams (83.5% vs 52.6%), scored substantially higher on all MCA subjects and on the ACT composite (private not-for-profit 4-year graduates score 5.4 ACT points higher than public 2-year graduates on average), are female, non-special education, and not economically disadvantaged. They are also more likely to have graduated from ACT-oriented high school programs with minimal CTE course-taking. They graduate from institutions outside Southwest Minnesota — either elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state — and as the bivariate workforce participation analysis showed, they are the group most likely to be working outside the region or outside Minnesota entirely a decade after graduation. The portrait of a sub-baccalaureate completer at a public 2-year institution within the Southwest Minnesota region is equally specific: they did not take the ACT (75.2% of non-ACT completers graduate from public 2-year institutions), are CTE Concentrators or Completors (46.8% public 2-year graduation rate vs 20.6% for No CTE completers), took significantly more CTE courses, scored lower on MCA subjects, are more likely to be male, more likely to be a special education student (78.6% of special education completers graduate from public 2-year institutions), more likely to be economically disadvantaged (51.7% public 2-year rate vs 30.9%), and more likely to be an English learner (69.8% public 2-year rate). They graduate from institutions within the Southwest Minnesota region, and as the workforce participation analysis showed, they are the group most likely to be working in the region a decade after graduation. Geography matters more at this stage than for attendance and graduation. EDR of origin is the strongest single predictor of graduation location (Cramer's V=0.179), with EDR 8 Southwest completers showing the highest out-of-state graduation rate (40.8%) and EDR 6E Southwest Central completers showing the strongest regional retention (36.0% regional graduation). This is the only stage of the postsecondary pathway where geographic origin within Southwest Minnesota meaningfully shapes outcomes, and it has direct implications for subregional workforce planning. ## **The Two Pathways** Taken together, the postsecondary pathway analysis reveals two distinct and consistently divergent pathways through which Southwest Minnesota high school graduates move into the workforce. The academic pathway is characterized by ACT participation, AP exam, PSEO, high MCA scores, non-special education status, economic advantage, and female gender. It leads through postsecondary attendance and graduation to bachelor degree or higher credentials at public or private 4-year institutions outside the Southwest Minnesota region and ultimately to employment outside the region or outside Minnesota entirely. The CTE pathway is characterized by CTE engagement, lower academic achievement indicators, special education status, economic disadvantage, English learner or non-English home language status, and male gender. It leads to either direct workforce entry without postsecondary or to sub-baccalaureate credentials at regional public 2-year institutions and ultimately to employment within the Southwest Minnesota region. These two pathways are not hierarchical in value — they serve fundamentally different workforce functions and both are essential to the Southwest Minnesota regional economy. But they are strikingly distinct in who follows them and where they lead, and understanding them as parallel systems rather than a single ladder is essential to designing effective regional education and workforce development policy.
